titre: Color, Center: American Spelling as a Political Project
accroche: Honor without the u, center rather than centre: for Noah Webster, an American spelling was first of all a political project.
contenu_vulgarise:
Colour becomes color, centre becomes center, honour becomes honor: American English spells a whole set of words differently from British English, by dropping a letter or swapping two. People often file this under spelling oddities, as if someone one day just found it simpler to write that way. The lexicographer Noah Webster, who popularized these forms (he didn't invent them; he chose among spellings that already existed), didn't present things that way.

## A Language of Its Own for an Independent Country

In 1789, six years after the treaty that ended the War of Independence, Webster published his *Dissertations on the English Language*. In it he wrote: “As an independent nation, our honor requires us to have a system of our own, in language as well as government.” He adds that Great Britain, “whose children we are and whose language we speak, should no longer be our model.” The argument isn't aesthetic: it's political. “Our political harmony is therefore concerned with a uniformity of language,” he writes, and several circumstances make a future separation of the American language from the English, in his view, “necessary and inevitable.”

The appendix to the same book, an essay on spelling reform, applies the reasoning to the letters themselves. Webster lists several advantages of a reformed spelling there: children and foreigners would learn more easily, pronunciation would be uniform across the United States, and books would cost one-eighteenth less to print. But the advantage he judges “chief” is another: an American spelling different from English spelling would be “of vast political consequence,” because English books could no longer serve both countries and printing would have to be done in America. “A national language is a bond of national union,” he adds, and he says he uses *luster*, *meter*, *theater*, or *sepulcher* in all his writings.

## From Pamphlet to Dictionary

This conviction took nearly 40 years to result in the work that would bear his name. In 1828, Webster published his *American Dictionary of the English Language*, in two quarto volumes, from S. Converse in New York: roughly 60,000 to 70,000 entries. It includes color, center, and honor, and the entry for *wagon* notes that the older spelling, waggon, “seems to be falling into disuse.” But Webster went further than what usage kept. In 1790, he printed a collection of essays in a reformed spelling: there one reads *tung* for tongue, *bilt* for built, *hed* for head, *helth* for health, *rong* for wrong, *munth* for month. None of these forms entered usage.

## What Usage Kept

The uneven fate of these proposals says something important about spelling reform in general: political motivation, even asserted with the force of a national manifesto, doesn't alone decide what a language keeps. Webster wanted an American spelling because he wanted an American identity; color stuck, tung didn't. What we write today without thinking, color or center, thus bears the trace of an 18th-century political project. How many other spellings today are the remnant of a choice of the same kind?

quiz.question: In his 1789 essay on spelling reform, which advantage does Webster call “chief”?
choix: The ease of learning spelling for children and foreigners
An American spelling distinct from English, of vast political consequence
A savings of about one-eighteenth on the cost of printing books
A uniform pronunciation across the United States
quiz.explication: Webster first lists ease of learning, uniformity of pronunciation, and savings on books: these are real arguments in the essay, but he doesn't call them chief. The “chief” advantage is that an American spelling different from the English would be “of vast political consequence”: English books would no longer serve both countries and printing would have to be done in America.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Noah Webster argue in his Dissertations on the English Language of 1789?
choix: That British spelling must remain the reference to unify the Empire
That the American language should move closer to French to mark its independence
That the United States, as an independent nation, must have a system of its own in language as well as government
That only an official academy can decide spelling
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Webster writes that, as an independent nation, the honor of the United States demands a system of its own in language as well as government, and that Great Britain should no longer be their model.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which spelling forms does Webster use in his 1790 collection of essays, and what happened to them afterward?
choix: Color, center, honor: all became the American standard
Colour, centre, honour: he returns to British spelling
Wagon, waggon: he hesitates between the two forms without deciding
Tung, bilt, hed, helth, rong, munth: none entered usage
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In his 1790 collection, Webster writes tung for tongue, bilt for built, hed for head, helth for health, rong for wrong, and munth for month; none of these radical forms entered usage, unlike color or center.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is the American Dictionary of the English Language, published by Webster in 1828?
choix: A dictionary in two quarto volumes from S. Converse in New York, with roughly 60,000 to 70,000 entries
A small pocket lexicon, limited to the reformed-spelling words Webster had proposed in 1790
An expanded reissue of the 1789 Dissertations, without a single dictionary entry
A dictionary published in England by a London publisher, to unify the two spellings
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In 1828 Webster publishes a dictionary in two quarto volumes, from S. Converse in New York, with roughly 60,000 to 70,000 entries, including color, center, and honor.
